design_detail: Cochrane systematic review with meta-analysis (CD005063.pub3, published March 2010; an update, by a new author team and with changed conclusions, of the 2005 Cochrane review by Ntais et al., whose protocol was published in Issue 1, 2005) of randomized and controlled clinical trials of benzodiazepines for alcohol withdrawal against placebo, other medicines, other benzodiazepines or benzodiazepine combinations, with a fifth comparison of fixed against symptom-triggered schedules. RevMan risk ratios (Mantel-Haenszel) and mean differences (inverse variance); every analysis in the Data and analyses tables is labelled random effects, although the Methods specify a fixed-effect model unless heterogeneity was significant. Searches to December 2009. 64 studies with 4309 participants by the review's count (65 entries in the characteristics table); all included studies were randomized trials, published from 1967 to 2009. The PMC version read carries the assigned DOI.
can_establish: Whether benzodiazepines, in randomized trials published up to 2009, changed the risk of withdrawal seizures, delirium, adverse events and drop-out during treatment of alcohol withdrawal compared with placebo or with other medicines, and how well those trials were conducted and reported.
cannot_establish: Whether benzodiazepines reduce withdrawal symptom severity compared with placebo (no such outcome was pooled); whether one benzodiazepine, dose or schedule is better than another (single small trials, doses not comparable); whether benzodiazepines are superior or equivalent to any particular other medicine (comparators from a dozen drug classes, plus ethanol and thiamine, were pooled as 'other drug'); outcomes after the withdrawal episode; effects in the people the trials mostly excluded (severe liver, heart, lung or kidney disease, other drug dependence); or anything from trials after December 2009.

sample.recruitment: Cochrane Drugs and Alcohol Group register of trials (December 2009), PubMed (1966 to December 2009), EMBASE (1988 to December 2009), CINAHL (1982 to December 2009) and EconLIT (1969 to December 2009), plus reference lists, conference proceedings and contact with investigators about unpublished trials; no language restriction (likely eligible non-English reports were translated). 695 reports screened, 91 full texts assessed (Results › Description of studies › Results of the search). Trials were from Europe (26), North America (32), Asia (3), South Africa (2) and Australia (1) (Results › Included studies). Participants came mostly from hospital wards, detoxification and rehabilitation units, psychiatric hospitals and Veterans Administration hospitals; the review says a clear understanding of the treatment setting was often impossible (Discussion › Quality of the evidence).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Included (Methods › Criteria for considering studies): RCTs and controlled clinical trials of benzodiazepines alone or combined with other drugs against placebo, other pharmacological treatment or other benzodiazepines, in people with alcohol dependence diagnosed by standardized criteria (DSM or ICD) who had withdrawal symptoms of any severity, regardless of age, sex, nationality or inpatient or outpatient treatment. All included studies were RCTs (Results › Risk of bias in included studies). Several included trials fall outside the stated population (Characteristics of included studies): Spies 2003 enrolled people meeting DSM-IV criteria for alcohol abuse and excluded those diagnosed with dependence; Saitz 1994 enrolled DSM-III-R abuse or dependence; Ansoms 1991 treated insomnia at least ten days after withdrawal; Kolin 1981, McLendon 1980, Mielke 1976 and Overall 1973 treated anxiety or depression after detoxification, from about five to 14 days after the last drink.
sample.demographics: Trials were small: 16 to 537 participants (Longo 2002 to Kaim 1969), most under 100. Many enrolled only men (Veterans Administration and other all-male samples); age limits of 18 to 65 were common and some trials excluded people over 55 (Kaim 1969, Brown 1972). People with severe liver, heart, lung or kidney disease, epilepsy or dependence on other drugs were commonly excluded (Characteristics of included studies; Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence).
sample.attrition: Not applicable at review level. Within trials, the review judged incomplete outcome data addressed in 48, unclear in 13 and not addressed in 3 (Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Incomplete outcome data). In the largest trial (Kaim 1969; 106 of 537 ended early), the seizure analysis (Analysis 1.1) uses 103 chlordiazepoxide and 130 placebo participants, while the drop-out analysis (Analysis 1.3) uses 117 and 156; the differences equal that trial's drop-outs in Analysis 1.3 (14, and 26 as far as the low-resolution image can be read), which suggests the seizure outcome was analysed only in those who stayed in the trial (editors' arithmetic).
sample.selection_effects: The evidence is old (most trials from 1967 to the 1990s), small and largely from inpatient or specialized settings, with medically complicated patients and people with other drug dependence excluded; three trials were in intensive-care patients (Spies 1996, multiply injured trauma patients; Lenzenhuber 1999; Spies 2003). Some trials studied anxiety, insomnia or mood after detoxification rather than acute withdrawal. No trial registry was searched, and small-study effects were not assessed.

exposure.measurement: Randomized allocation to a benzodiazepine: chlordiazepoxide, diazepam, lorazepam, oxazepam, alprazolam, clobazam, clorazepate, flunitrazepam, halazepam, lormetazepam (spelled 'Lometazepam' in the review), lopirazepam and prazepam, plus the compound the review lists as 'Abecamil' (Anton 1997) (Results › Included studies; Table 5).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions only, as the review reports them: oral, intramuscular and intravenous routes; fixed tapering, loading, front-loading and symptom-triggered schedules; treatment from a few hours (Naranjo 1983) to three weeks or more (Saletu 1983). The authors state they could not examine dose-response because patients were not treated with similar doses across trials (Discussion › Quality of the evidence). The three schedule trials compared fixed and symptom-triggered oxazepam (Daeppen 2002) and chlordiazepoxide (Saitz 1994), and, in intensive care, a flunitrazepam-clonidine-haloperidol combination titrated by continuous infusion or by boluses (Spies 2003).
exposure.polysubstance: Most trials excluded dependence on other drugs and recent use of benzodiazepines or other psychotropic medicines. Concomitant medicines were allowed in some trials and not standardized: phenytoin for people with a history of withdrawal seizures in both arms of Sellers 1983, extra diazepam when needed in Bailly 1992, additional doses at the clinician's judgement in Radouco-Thomas 1989, vitamins in several (Characteristics of included studies).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: outcomes were measured during the withdrawal episode, or over the following weeks in the post-detoxification anxiety and insomnia trials.

comparison.controls: Placebo (11 trials, several with supportive care); other drugs (42 trials by the review's count, Tables 2 to 4): anticonvulsant or sedative drugs (chlormethiazole, carbamazepine, valproate, barbiturates, paraldehyde, magnesium sulphate, topiramate, lamotrigine, gabapentin), antipsychotics (chlorpromazine, perphenazine, thioridazine, mesoridazine, haloperidol, tiapride, melperone, cyamemazine), propranolol, clonidine, GHB, baclofen, bromocriptine, hydroxyzine, benzoctamine, zopiclone, memantine, nitrous oxide, ethanol and thiamine; other benzodiazepines (18 trials); combinations (3); different schedules of the same benzodiazepine (3).
comparison.matching: Randomization within trials. Sequence generation was adequate in 16 trials, unclear in 43 and inadequate in 5; allocation concealment adequate in 13, unclear in 47 and inadequate in 4 (Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Allocation). Some trials described as randomized allocated by rotation or order of admission (Golbert 1967, Overall 1973, Lucht 2003).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable at review level. Withdrawal severity at entry, past withdrawal seizures or delirium, liver disease and co-occurring illness differed between trials and could not be examined; the authors note that harms data came from patients with potentially different comorbidity (Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence).
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Comparators came from the same trial populations. Within the pooled 'other drug' comparisons, some comparators were sedatives or anticonvulsants while others were not active treatments for withdrawal (the thiamine and hydroxyzine arms of Kaim 1969; ethanol in Golbert 1967 and Funderburk 1978).

outcomes.instruments: Withdrawal seizures and delirium (participants with the event); withdrawal severity on the CIWA-Ar or other scales (Gross scale, Total Severity Assessment, AWAS); anxiety on the Hamilton Anxiety Rating Scale (HARS) or the Zung scale; global improvement and physicians' and patients' global assessments; participants with at least one adverse event or a severe life-threatening adverse event; mortality; drop-out and drop-out due to adverse events (Methods › Types of outcome measures).
outcomes.validity_norms: Rating scales differed between trials; only trials with exactly the same scale or the same binary outcome were pooled, and the authors name the variety of outcomes and scales as the main limit on quantitative synthesis (Results › Effects of interventions; Discussion › Summary of main results).
outcomes.operationalization: Primary efficacy outcomes: seizures, delirium, symptom scores, global improvement and craving; safety: adverse events and severe life-threatening adverse events; acceptability: drop-out and drop-out for adverse events; secondary: additional medication, intensive-care stay, mortality, quality of life. The review does not say whether the CIWA-Ar and HARS values it pooled are scores at the stated time point or changes from baseline: the Methods mention imputing standard deviations for changes from baseline, the Discussion speaks of change from baseline, and the analysis titles say only 'score'.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None. 40 counts the outcome analyses in the Data and analyses tables (Comparison 1, 4; Comparison 2, 15; Comparison 3, 12; Comparison 4, 3; Comparison 5, 6), many with two or more subgroups and most in Comparisons 3 to 5 based on a single trial.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Blinding for subjective outcomes was judged adequate in 43 trials, unclear in 14 and inadequate in 7; for objective outcomes adequate in 52 and unclear in 12 (Results › Risk of bias in included studies › Blinding). Where a trial did not say whether assessors were blinded, the review assumed that outcomes recorded during treatment were assessed by the blinded staff who gave it, a note repeated in most entries of the Characteristics of included studies.

analysis.effect_sizes: Against placebo: seizures RR 0.16 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.69), 3 trials, 324 participants, 1 of 149 against 14 of 175 (Kaim 1969, 1/103 against 9/130; Naranjo 1983, 0/21 against 1/20; Sellers 1983, 0/25 against 4/25), I2 0%, GRADE moderate, illustrative 80 against 13 per 1000; adverse events RR 3.28 (0.31 to 34.52), 2 trials, 71, 6 against 1 events, low; drop-out RR 0.68 (0.38 to 1.24), 3 trials, 312, moderate; drop-out for adverse events RR 0.36 (0.02 to 8.03), 2 trials, 86. Against other drugs: seizures RR 0.52 (0.21 to 1.31), 12 trials, 1228, 5 of 442 against 37 of 786, moderate; against anticonvulsants RR 1.70 (0.39 to 7.37), 7 trials, 523, 4 of 244 against 2 of 279; delirium RR 0.65 (0.21 to 1.98), 8 trials, 893, I2 52%; against anticonvulsants RR 1.90 (0.43 to 8.38), 5 trials, 342, 13 of 159 against 7 of 183; CIWA-Ar at 48 hours MD -1.03 (-2.21 to 0.15), 5 trials, 355, and at end of treatment MD -0.17 (-1.29 to 0.95), 6 trials, 435 (against anticonvulsants -0.73, -2.88 to 1.42, and -1.04, -3.45 to 1.38, 3 trials, 260); HARS at 48 hours MD -1.60 (-2.59 to -0.61), 1 trial, 43, and at end of treatment MD -2.05 (-4.37 to 0.27), 2 trials, 90, I2 56%; Zung anxiety MD 0.80 (-24.18 to 22.58), 1 trial, 136; global improvement RR 1.01 (0.90 to 1.12), 11 trials, 619 (against anticonvulsants 1.00, 0.87 to 1.16); physicians' assessment RR 1.04 (0.97 to 1.11), 3 trials, 233; patients' assessment RR 1.04 (0.97 to 1.12), 2 trials, 140; adverse events RR 1.31 (0.99 to 1.72), 18 trials, 919, 93 of 426 against 69 of 493, low (against anticonvulsants 1.50, 0.83 to 2.70, 9 trials, 471, rated high); severe life-threatening adverse events RR 1.95 (0.25 to 15.28), 7 trials, 340, 2 against 1 events (against anticonvulsants 1.45, 0.19 to 11.24); drop-out RR 0.93 (0.70 to 1.24), 22 trials, 1848, moderate (against anticonvulsants 1.11, 0.75 to 1.63, 11 trials, 839, rated high); drop-out for adverse events RR 0.82 (0.23 to 2.88), 8 trials, 533; deaths in 4 of the 32 trials in the mortality analysis, not pooled. Between benzodiazepines: single trials of 20 to 100 participants, none significant except HARS at end of treatment, alprazolam against chlordiazepoxide MD -2.90 (-4.10 to -1.70), 43, and lopirazepam against prazepam MD 1.60 (0.39 to 2.81), 42. Fixed against symptom-triggered schedules: CIWA-Ar at 48 hours MD -5.70 (-11.02 to -0.38), 1 trial (Spies 2003), 44; at end of treatment MD -1.10 (-3.27 to 1.07), Daeppen 2002, 117, and MD 1.00 (-2.47 to 4.47), Spies 2003, 44; delirium RR 3.06 (0.33 to 28.44), Saitz 1994, 101; seizures RR 0.31 (0.01 to 7.37), Daeppen 2002, 117. No tau-squared or prediction intervals in the text; heterogeneity statistics appear only in the forest-plot images. Per-trial counts above were read from the forest-plot images and agree with the printed totals.
analysis.covariates: Not applicable (aggregate trial data; no meta-regression).
analysis.preregistration_detail: Cochrane protocol first published in Issue 1, 2005; review first published in Issue 3, 2005; this version updated in January 2010 with new authors and changed conclusions (What's new; History). There is no 'Differences between protocol and review' section. Deviations visible in the article: all analyses are labelled random effects although the Methods specify fixed effect unless heterogeneity was significant; a fifth comparison (fixed against symptom-triggered schedules) is analysed that the Methods' list of four comparisons does not include; only four of the six Cochrane risk-of-bias domains were assessed.
analysis.selective_reporting: Data from comparisons that could not be pooled were not synthesized and are mostly not reported numerically (Results › Effects of interventions, 1st paragraph). Craving, additional medication, length of intensive-care stay and quality of life are listed as outcomes but not reported. Selective outcome reporting within trials was not assessed.
analysis.power: Not addressed. The placebo seizure result rests on 15 events, the seizure comparison with other drugs on 42 (27 of them in the comparator arms of one trial), and the severe adverse event comparison on 3; most comparisons between benzodiazepines and between schedules are single trials of 20 to 117 participants.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Against placebo, three trials with 324 participants and 15 seizures in all showed fewer withdrawal seizures with benzodiazepines (RR 0.16, 0.04 to 0.69); no other placebo-controlled outcome differed, and no withdrawal-severity outcome was pooled against placebo. Against other drugs no pooled outcome differed significantly: seizures and delirium tended to favour benzodiazepines, while adverse events tended to be more frequent with benzodiazepines (RR 1.31, 0.99 to 1.72), and against anticonvulsants the seizure and delirium point estimates favoured the anticonvulsants. Comparisons between benzodiazepines and between schedules rest on single small trials.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that benzodiazepines "showed a protective benefit against alcohol withdrawal symptoms, in particular seizures" against placebo, and a potentially protective benefit for many outcomes against other drugs (Abstract › Authors' conclusions; Implications for practice). Gaps: (1) no symptom-severity outcome was pooled against placebo, so the benefit against symptoms rests on seizures alone; (2) the abstract lists severe life-threatening side effects among the trends favouring benzodiazepines, whereas Analysis 2.12 has 2 such events with benzodiazepines and 1 with other drugs (RR 1.95, 0.25 to 15.28, on the side the plot labels as favouring other drugs), and the abstract leaves out the borderline excess of adverse events with benzodiazepines shown in Summary of findings 2; (3) the abstract gives its one significant comparison as a trial of 61 participants, but the analysis has 43 (Baumgartner 1991; 61 is the size of Baumgartner 1987); (4) for fixed against symptom-triggered schedules the abstract presents a non-significant single-trial result (MD -1.10, -3.27 to 1.07) as favouring symptom-triggered dosing and gives it 159 participants, when the analysis has 117 (Daeppen 2002), while the only significant result (MD -5.70) comes from 44 intensive-care patients given a flunitrazepam-clonidine-haloperidol combination by infusion or by boluses (Spies 2003); (5) the statement that chlordiazepoxide performed better rests on non-significant single trials; (6) the Discussion counts 57 RCTs and over 4000 patients against 64 studies and 4309 elsewhere. Against this, the abstract also says no definite conclusions were possible, and the Discussion is restrained about comparisons with other drugs.

timeline.event: Mayo-Smith meta-analysis and practice guideline, cited by this review as finding benzodiazepines effective in reducing withdrawal severity, delirium and seizures, with a greater margin of safety than other treatments
Holbrook et al. meta-analysis of benzodiazepines in acute alcohol withdrawal (CMAJ), cited as reaching similar conclusions.
First Cochrane version (Ntais, Pakos, Kyzas and Ioannidis, 2005; protocol Issue 1, 2005), whose results this update describes as not conclusive.
This update: new author team, search to December 2009, conclusions changed.
Parallel Cochrane review of anticonvulsants for alcohol withdrawal by the same authors (Minozzi, Amato, Vecchi and Davoli, 2010), cited; Tier B of the alcohol list (Minozzi 2010, CD005064.pub3).

replication.where_it_stands: The standard Cochrane source for placebo-controlled seizure prevention with benzodiazepines in alcohol withdrawal, but that result rests on three trials from 1969 to 1983 with 15 seizures in all, and the search ends in December 2009. Its comparisons with other medicines pool unlike comparators and are imprecise, so they show neither superiority nor equivalence. The PMC record links no correction or later version; whether Cochrane has published a later version was not checked in this reading. Claims about fixed against symptom-triggered dosing should be anchored in the primary trials (Saitz 1994 is on Tier B of the list; Daeppen 2002), not in this review's single-trial analyses. Mayo-Smith (1997) is cited here as background and is not part of the pooled data.

funding.funder: Internal: Department of Epidemiology, ASL RM/E, Rome, Italy. External: AIFA (Italian Pharmaceutical Agency), Italy, described as a public regulatory agency for medicinal products (Sources of support).
funding.affiliations_note: All four authors are at the Department of Epidemiology, ASL RM/E, Rome; the review was published under the Cochrane Drugs and Alcohol Group. Vecchi ran the searches; Minozzi and Vecchi reviewed the papers and extracted data; Minozzi wrote the methods and results and assessed trial quality; Amato wrote the abstract, introduction and discussion; Davoli supervised (Contributions of authors). Funding of the included trials was not recorded; one trial used a randomization table supplied by its sponsor (Runion 1978).

what_would_settle_it: Adequately powered, concealed and blinded trials, or an individual-participant meta-analysis of the existing ones, in people at defined risk of complicated withdrawal, with prespecified seizure, delirium, serious-harm and mortality outcomes and one symptom scale reported both as end-point and change scores; for dosing strategy, trials of symptom-triggered against fixed schedules of a benzodiazepine alone, on general wards and in intensive care, with seizures and delirium as primary outcomes.

domains.domain: 1. PICO components in research question and inclusion criteria
domains.note: Population (alcohol dependence with withdrawal), intervention (benzodiazepines alone or combined), comparators (placebo, other drugs, other benzodiazepines) and outcomes are specified.

Cochrane protocol published in 2005 before the first version; but this update reports no differences between protocol and review, and its visible deviations (random effects throughout despite a fixed-effect plan, an added schedule comparison, four of six risk-of-bias domains) are not justified.
RCTs and controlled clinical trials are named as eligible without a reason for the choice.

Five databases with strategies in appendices, reference lists, conference proceedings and investigator contact, no language restriction, search three months before publication; but no trial registries, and the published strategies are partly inconsistent (Appendix 1 is a CENTRAL strategy from The Cochrane Library 2004 while the Methods name the group's register; no EconLIT strategy is given).
Two authors independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed full texts.
Two authors independently extracted data, resolving differences by discussion.

domains.domain: 7. List of excluded studies with justification (critical)
domains.note: All 27 excluded full texts are listed with a reason each (Characteristics of excluded studies).

domains.domain: 8. Included studies described in adequate detail
domains.note: Participants, inclusion and exclusion criteria, arms and outcomes are given for each trial; setting, follow-up period and doses are often missing (the authors say settings were often unclear).

domains.domain: 9. Satisfactory risk-of-bias assessment of included studies (critical)
domains.note: Cochrane tool for sequence generation, concealment, blinding (subjective and objective outcomes) and incomplete data, with support for each judgment; selective reporting and other bias were not assessed, and assessor blinding was assumed whenever the treating staff were blinded.

domains.domain: 10. Funding sources of included studies reported

domains.note: Risk ratios and mean differences with random effects are suitable in themselves, but the review states it pooled only directly comparable interventions and then pooled benzodiazepines against any other drug (anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, beta-blockers, clonidine, GHB, baclofen, nitrous oxide, ethanol, thiamine) in single estimates; in the seizure pool the comparator arm of Kaim 1969 combines chlorpromazine, hydroxyzine and thiamine and holds 27 of the 37 comparator events; the same trial (Malcolm 1989) is entered with different standard deviations in two subgroups of Analysis 2.3; and Comparison 4 mislabels its arms.

domains.domain: 12. Impact of risk of bias on pooled results assessed
domains.note: Forest plots were sorted by risk of bias (concealment) and inspected; no systematic difference was found, so the planned sensitivity analysis was not run. A lenient reading: the inspection is reported only as a sentence.

domains.domain: 13. Risk of bias accounted for in interpretation (critical)
domains.note: GRADE ratings in both summary-of-findings tables and a Quality of the evidence section stating that bias cannot be excluded and concealment was usually unclear.

Statistical heterogeneity was low in most pools (I2 0% for seizures); the clinical heterogeneity of interventions and scales is discussed as the reason no definite conclusions are possible, and anticonvulsant comparators are analysed as a subgroup.
Funnel plots were not used, on the grounds that all trials were small with non-significant results; publication bias is neither investigated nor discussed.

domains.domain: 16. Conflicts of interest and funding reported
domains.note: Sources of support and declarations of interest are given.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Two critical items are 'no' (11: pooling of unlike comparators against the review's own rule, with data-entry inconsistencies; 15: publication bias not investigated), which under AMSTAR 2 gives critically low confidence; critical items 2, 4 and 9 are partly met and 7 and 13 met. On a lenient reading of item 11 the rating would be low confidence, because item 15 alone is a critical flaw. This rates the review as a summary, not the trials: for the trials the card follows the review's own appraisal and says so (concealment unclear or inadequate in 51 of 64, sequence generation unclear or inadequate in 48). The review may be cited for the inventory of randomized trials to December 2009, for the placebo-controlled seizure result with its fragility (1 against 14 events in three trials from 1969 to 1983; GRADE moderate by the review), for the absence of demonstrated differences from other medicines (imprecise; not equivalence), and for the sparse harms data; it should not be cited for an effect of benzodiazepines on withdrawal severity against placebo, for comparisons between benzodiazepines, for the direction of the CIWA-Ar and HARS comparisons with other drugs, or for the benefit of symptom-triggered dosing.

key_findings.finding: 64 studies with 4309 participants met the inclusion criteria, all randomized trials: 11 against placebo, 42 against other drugs, 18 comparing benzodiazepines and 3 comparing a benzodiazepine alone with a combination (some multi-arm trials in more than one), plus 3 trials of fixed against symptom-triggered schedules. 695 reports were screened, 91 full texts assessed, 27 excluded with reasons and 1 awaits classification. Trials came from North America (32), Europe (26), Asia (3), South Africa (2) and Australia (1).
key_findings.locator: Abstract › Main results; Results › Description of studies › Results of the search; Included studies (comparison lists and Tables 1 to 6); Results › Effects of interventions, fixed versus symptom-triggered paragraph
key_findings.note: The characteristics table has 65 entries (Burroughs 1985a and 1985b are two severity strata of one publication; Pena-Ramos 1977 and 1979 report the same participants), and its participant numbers sum to 4631 (editors' arithmetic); the Discussion says 57 RCTs and over 4000 patients.

key_findings.finding: Against placebo, benzodiazepines were associated with fewer withdrawal seizures: RR 0.16 (95% CI 0.04 to 0.69), 3 trials (Kaim 1969, chlordiazepoxide; Naranjo 1983, lorazepam; Sellers 1983, diazepam), 324 participants, 1 seizure in 149 against 14 in 175 (1/103 against 9/130; 0/21 against 1/20; 0/25 against 4/25), I2 0%, test for overall effect P = 0.014. GRADE moderate, downgraded because allocation concealment was unclear in 2 of the 3 trials; illustrative risk 80 per 1000 with placebo against 13 per 1000 (3 to 55).
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 1, 1.1 Alcohol withdrawal seizures; Data and analyses, Comparison 1; Analysis 1.1 (forest-plot image)
key_findings.note: Per-trial counts were read from the Analysis 1.1 image (566 pixels wide, enlarged on screen) and add up to the printed totals. No single trial was significant on its own (Kaim 1969, RR 0.14, 0.02 to 1.09). The image labels the largest trial 'Kaim 1972', but its group sizes are those of Kaim 1969. In Sellers 1983 everyone with past withdrawal seizures also received phenytoin. The 1997 review (Mayo-Smith; sc_mayo_smith_1997, Table 2) gives Naranjo 1983 as 0 of 15 against 2 of 15, not 0 of 21 against 1 of 20; neither review explains the difference.

key_findings.finding: Against placebo, no other outcome differed: adverse events RR 3.28 (0.31 to 34.52), 2 trials, 71 participants, 6 against 1 events (5 of 25 on diazepam against 0 of 25 on placebo in Krupitsky 2007), GRADE low; drop-out RR 0.68 (0.38 to 1.24), 3 trials, 312, GRADE moderate; drop-out for adverse events RR 0.36 (0.02 to 8.03), 2 trials, 86. No pooled analysis of withdrawal symptom severity against placebo was reported.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings for the main comparison; Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 1, 1.2 to 1.4; Analysis 1.2 (forest-plot image)

key_findings.finding: Against other drugs, seizures did not differ: RR 0.52 (0.21 to 1.31), 12 trials, 1228 participants, 5 of 442 against 37 of 786, I2 0%, GRADE moderate; 27 of the 37 comparator seizures occurred in one trial (Kaim 1969, 1/103 against 27/304), whose comparator arm combines chlorpromazine, hydroxyzine and thiamine. Against anticonvulsants the point estimate favoured the anticonvulsants: RR 1.70 (0.39 to 7.37), 7 trials, 523, 4 of 244 against 2 of 279, GRADE moderate.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 2; Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 2, 2.1.1 and 2.1.2; Analysis 2.1 (forest-plot image)
key_findings.note: Per-trial counts read from the Analysis 2.1 image; they add up to the printed subtotals (442 and 786; 244 and 279).

key_findings.finding: Delirium did not differ: against any other drug RR 0.65 (0.21 to 1.98), 8 trials, 893 participants, 14 events in 321 on benzodiazepines, I2 52% (P = 0.04); against anticonvulsants RR 1.90 (0.43 to 8.38), 5 trials, 342, 13 of 159 against 7 of 183, I2 42%. The largest weight in both (about 25%) is Golbert 1967, which allocated by rotation.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 2, 2.2.1 and 2.2.2; Analysis 2.2 (forest-plot image); Characteristics of included studies, Golbert 1967

key_findings.finding: Symptom and anxiety scores against other drugs: CIWA-Ar at 48 hours MD -1.03 (-2.21 to 0.15), 5 trials, 355; at end of treatment MD -0.17 (-1.29 to 0.95), 6 trials, 435; against anticonvulsants MD -0.73 (-2.88 to 1.42) and -1.04 (-3.45 to 1.38), 3 trials, 260. HARS at 48 hours MD -1.60 (-2.59 to -0.61), 1 trial (Baumgartner 1991: chlordiazepoxide 20, mean 8.6, SD 1.6, against transdermal clonidine 23, mean 10.2, SD 1.7); at end of treatment MD -2.05 (-4.37 to 0.27), 2 trials, 90, I2 56%. The review reads all negative differences as favouring the comparator.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 2, 2.3 to 2.6; Data and analyses, Comparison 2; Analyses 2.3, 2.5 and 2.6 (forest-plot images)
key_findings.note: Direction unverified: the forest plots label negative differences as favouring other drugs or clonidine, which is right only if the values are reductions from baseline; the review never says whether it pooled end-point scores or changes (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Global outcomes against other drugs showed no difference: global improvement RR 1.01 (0.90 to 1.12), 11 trials, 619 (against anticonvulsants 1.00, 0.87 to 1.16, 6 trials, 338); physicians' global assessment RR 1.04 (0.97 to 1.11), 3 trials, 233; patients' global assessment RR 1.04 (0.97 to 1.12), 2 trials, 140. The authors state that the intervals exclude clinically meaningful differences in these broadly defined success rates.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 2, 2.8 to 2.10; Discussion › Summary of main results, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Safety against other drugs: participants with at least one adverse event RR 1.31 (0.99 to 1.72), 18 trials, 919, 93 of 426 against 69 of 493, GRADE low (concealment adequate in 6 of 18); against anticonvulsants RR 1.50 (0.83 to 2.70), 9 trials, 471, GRADE high; severe life-threatening adverse events RR 1.95 (0.25 to 15.28), 7 trials, 340, 2 events with benzodiazepines (Burroughs 1985b, 1 of 10; Tubridy 1988, 1 of 46) against 1 with other drugs (Tubridy 1988, 1 of 44); against anticonvulsants RR 1.45 (0.19 to 11.24), 5 trials, 230.
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 2; Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 2, 2.11 and 2.12; Analyses 2.11 and 2.12 (forest-plot images)
key_findings.note: The 'high' GRADE rating for adverse events against anticonvulsants is given to an interval running from a 17% reduction to a 2.7-fold increase; the summary-of-findings table does not say why it was not downgraded for imprecision.

key_findings.finding: Mortality against other drugs was analysed in 32 trials (2088 participants) and not pooled; deaths occurred in 4: Golbert 1967 (0 of 12 against 2 of 37), Kaim 1969 (0 of 103 against 2 of 304), Kaim 1972 (0 of 46 against 1 of 142) and Lenzenhuber 1999, an intensive-care trial (2 of 21 on flunitrazepam against 0 of 21 on GHB). The authors call the mortality rate extremely small and reassuring, and harms data sparse and fragmented.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 2, 2.13 Mortality; Analysis 2.13 (forest-plot image); Discussion › Overall completeness and applicability of evidence
key_findings.note: The text says only 4 of 21 studies reported deaths; the analysis lists 32 trials.

key_findings.finding: Acceptability against other drugs: drop-out RR 0.93 (0.70 to 1.24), 22 trials, 1848, GRADE moderate (against anticonvulsants RR 1.11, 0.75 to 1.63, 11 trials, 839, GRADE high); drop-out for adverse events RR 0.82 (0.23 to 2.88), 8 trials, 533 (against anticonvulsants RR 0.54, 0.14 to 2.16, 6 trials, 370).
key_findings.locator: Summary of findings 2; Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 2, 2.14 and 2.15

key_findings.finding: Between benzodiazepines, every comparison rested on one to three trials (20 to 158 participants) and none differed on seizures, delirium, CIWA-Ar, global assessments, adverse events or drop-out (for example seizures, chlordiazepoxide against alprazolam, RR 0.44, 0.15 to 1.35, 100 participants). Two single trials differed on HARS at end of treatment: alprazolam against chlordiazepoxide MD -2.90 (-4.10 to -1.70), 43 (McLendon 1980), read by the review as favouring chlordiazepoxide; lopirazepam against prazepam MD 1.60 (0.39 to 2.81), 42 (Saletu 1983), read as favouring lopirazepam. The authors conclude there is no strong evidence that particular benzodiazepines are more effective.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions › Comparison 3, 3.1 to 3.12; Data and analyses, Comparison 3; Discussion › Summary of main results, 4th paragraph

key_findings.finding: Fixed against symptom-triggered schedules (3 trials, 262 participants): CIWA-Ar at 48 hours MD -5.70 (-11.02 to -0.38), P = 0.036, from Spies 2003 alone (21 infusion-titrated against 23 bolus-titrated intensive-care patients given flunitrazepam, clonidine and haloperidol; DSM-IV alcohol abuse); at end of treatment MD -1.10 (-3.27 to 1.07), Daeppen 2002, 117 (oxazepam), and MD 1.00 (-2.47 to 4.47), Spies 2003; delirium 3 of 50 on fixed against 1 of 51 on symptom-triggered chlordiazepoxide, RR 3.06 (0.33 to 28.44), Saitz 1994; seizures RR 0.31 (0.01 to 7.37), Daeppen 2002; deaths only in Spies 2003 (2 of 21 against 1 of 23). The authors call all other outcomes non-significant.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions, fixed versus symptom-triggered paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 5; Analyses 5.2 to 5.5 (forest-plot images); Characteristics of included studies, Daeppen 2002, Saitz 1994, Spies 2003
key_findings.note: The review labels the Spies 2003 arms 'flunitrazepam (fixed schedule)' and 'flunitrazepam (symptom-triggered)'; its own characteristics table describes them as infusion-titrated and bolus-titrated three-drug regimens.

key_findings.finding: Benzodiazepine alone against combinations (3 trials, 207 participants): mortality RR 0.86 (0.39 to 1.90), with all deaths in one trial of multiply injured patients in intensive care (Spies 1996: 15 of 109 in the two flunitrazepam combination arms against 8 of 50 on clomethiazole with haloperidol); drop-out RR 3.89 (0.51 to 29.91), 1 trial, 169; drop-out for adverse events RR 2.29 (0.28 to 19.12), 1 trial, 159. The authors call the data very limited.
key_findings.locator: Results › Effects of interventions, benzodiazepine plus other drug paragraph; Data and analyses, Comparison 4; Analysis 4.1 (forest-plot image); Characteristics of included studies, Spies 1996

key_findings.finding: Risk of bias of the 64 trials, as judged by the review: sequence generation adequate in 16, unclear in 43, inadequate in 5; allocation concealment adequate in 13, unclear in 47, inadequate in 4; blinding for subjective outcomes adequate in 43, unclear in 14, inadequate in 7; for objective outcomes adequate in 52, unclear in 12; incomplete outcome data addressed in 48, unclear in 13, not addressed in 3. Selective reporting and other bias were not assessed. Sorting forest plots by risk of bias showed no systematic difference, so no sensitivity analysis was done.
key_findings.locator: Results › Risk of bias in included studies (Allocation; Blinding; Incomplete outcome data; final paragraph); Methods › Assessment of risk of bias in included studies

key_findings.finding: Publication bias was not assessed: funnel plots were not used because all included studies were small with non-significant results. Small-trial size, poorly reported randomization, usually unclear concealment, missing follow-up information, unclear treatment settings and non-comparable doses are named by the authors as reasons for caution.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Assessment of reporting biases; Discussion › Quality of the evidence

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract attributes its one statistically significant comparison with other drugs (HARS, MD -1.60, -2.59 to -0.61) to a study with 61 participants; the results text and Analysis 2.5 give 1 study (Baumgartner 1991) with 43 participants (20 and 23). 61 is the number enrolled in Baumgartner 1987.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Main results; Results › Effects of interventions › 2.5; Analysis 2.5; Characteristics of included studies
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's sample size is wrong; claims must use 43 and name the trial.

reporting_issues.issue: For fixed against symptom-triggered schedules the abstract cites a single study with 159 participants and MD -1.10 (-3.27 to 1.07) at end of treatment as favouring symptom-triggered regimens; Analysis 5.4 gives that estimate for Daeppen 2002 with 117 participants, and the interval includes zero. The results text instead reports a significant benefit at 48 hours (MD -5.70, -11.02 to -0.38), which comes from Spies 2003 (44 intensive-care patients on a three-drug combination).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Main results; Results › Effects of interventions, fixed versus symptom-triggered paragraph; Analyses 5.3 and 5.4
reporting_issues.consequence: Neither the abstract nor the results text supports a general claim that symptom-triggered benzodiazepine dosing is superior; the primary trials must be read for that question.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract lists severe life-threatening side effects among the trends in favour of benzodiazepines against other drugs; Analysis 2.12 shows 2 events with benzodiazepines against 1 with other drugs, RR 1.95 (0.25 to 15.28), on the side the plot labels as favouring other drugs.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Main results; Results › Effects of interventions › 2.12; Analysis 2.12
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract misstates the direction of a safety outcome; claims on comparative safety must use the analysis (three events in all, no difference shown).

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods do not say whether the CIWA-Ar and HARS values pooled are end-point scores or changes from baseline. Two passages read them as changes (the Results paragraph on fixed against symptom-triggered schedules calls its 48-hour CIWA-Ar result a change from baseline, and the Discussion reads the HARS and doctors' global-assessment comparisons as changes from baseline), and the forest plots label a negative difference as favouring the comparator (other drugs, clonidine, symptom-triggered schedules), which is correct only for reductions from baseline; but the values printed do not all fit that reading: in Analysis 5.4 the values for Spies 2003 (19.8 and 18.8) are of the size of reductions from an entry score above 20, while those for Daeppen 2002 in the same analysis (2.8 and 3.9) could be either.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Measures of treatment effect; Results › Effects of interventions, fixed versus symptom-triggered paragraph; Discussion › Summary of main results, 3rd paragraph; Analyses 2.3, 2.5, 2.6, 5.3 and 5.4
reporting_issues.consequence: The direction of every continuous comparison (including the statement that benzodiazepines were, if anything, less effective than other drugs on anxiety) cannot be confirmed from the review; claims need the primary trials.

reporting_issues.issue: In Analysis 2.3 (CIWA-Ar at 48 hours) the same trial, Malcolm 1989, is entered with different standard deviations in the two subgroups (about 6.8 and 6.1 in the any-other-drug subgroup, 9.8 and 9.2 in the anticonvulsant subgroup), giving intervals of -5.11 to 1.11 and -6.58 to 2.58 for the same comparison (editors' check of the printed intervals against the standard deviations).
reporting_issues.consequence: A data-entry inconsistency; it does not change any conclusion, but it shows the pooled continuous data were not checked against each other.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods specify a fixed-effect model unless heterogeneity was significant, but every analysis in the Data and analyses tables is labelled random effects (M-H, Random; IV, Random), without explanation.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Data synthesis; Data and analyses, Comparisons 1 to 5
reporting_issues.consequence: An unexplained deviation from the stated methods; with I2 near 0% in most pools the estimates would differ little.

reporting_issues.issue: Comparison counts and lists do not match: the list of 'benzodiazepines versus other drug' studies, said to number 42, names 41; it includes Addolorato 2006, which Table 4 calls Addolorato 2005; Tables 2 and 4 include Thompson 1975, which is listed among the excluded studies, and Ansoms 1991, which is not in the list; the three schedule trials appear in no comparison list, and the mortality list names Malcolm 2002 twice (Analysis 2.13 shows Malcolm 1989 and 2002) and says 4 of 21 studies reported deaths while 32 are analysed.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Included studies (Number of studies per type of comparison; Tables 2 and 4); Characteristics of excluded studies; Results › Effects of interventions › 2.13; Analysis 2.13
reporting_issues.consequence: The study inventory cannot be reconstructed exactly from the text; trial counts in claims should be taken from the Data and analyses tables.

reporting_issues.issue: The participant count of 4309 cannot be reconciled with the characteristics table, whose 65 entries sum to 4631 participants (4597 without the second Pena-Ramos report; editors' arithmetic); some entries also disagree internally (Lucht 2003: 127 participants but arms of 34, 31 and 28; Addolorato 1999: 60 but arms of 22 and 26; Funderburk 1978: age range 22 to 45 with a mean of 45). The Discussion gives 57 RCTs and over 4000 patients.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract; Results › Included studies; Characteristics of included studies; Discussion › Summary of main results
reporting_issues.consequence: The total number of participants should be cited as the review's figure, not as an exact count.

reporting_issues.issue: Comparison 4 is titled 'benzodiazepine alone vs benzodiazepine + other drugs', but its only subgroup is labelled 'Benzodiazepine+Other Drug vs. Other Drug', and in Spies 1996 the 'benzodiazepine alone' column holds the two flunitrazepam combination arms (with haloperidol or with clonidine) while the 'benzodiazepine + other' column holds clomethiazole with haloperidol, which contains no benzodiazepine. The Methods and abstract describe the comparison as a benzodiazepine combined with another drug against the other drug.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Types of interventions; Abstract › Main results; Results › Effects of interventions, benzodiazepine plus other drug paragraph; Analysis 4.1; Table 6
reporting_issues.consequence: The mortality estimate in Comparison 4 (RR 0.86, 0.39 to 1.90, all deaths in one intensive-care trial) does not answer the question its title asks and should not be cited.

reporting_issues.issue: The forest plot of Analysis 1.1 labels the largest trial 'Kaim 1972', while the text names Kaim 1969 and the group sizes (103 and 130) are those of Kaim 1969 in the characteristics table (Kaim 1972 had 46 on chlordiazepoxide and 14 on placebo).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Analysis 1.1 (forest-plot image); Results › Effects of interventions › 1.1; Characteristics of included studies, Kaim 1969 and Kaim 1972
reporting_issues.consequence: A labelling error; the data are those of Kaim 1969.

reporting_issues.issue: The Zung anxiety estimate is printed as MD 0.80 with an interval of -24.18 to 22.58, whose midpoint is -0.80 (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Effects of interventions › 2.7
reporting_issues.consequence: A sign error in either the estimate or the interval; the single-trial result is null either way.

reporting_issues.issue: Search documentation is inconsistent: Appendix 1 is a CENTRAL strategy headed The Cochrane Library 4, 2004 (the first version's), while the Methods name the Cochrane Drugs and Alcohol Group register searched in December 2009; no EconLIT strategy is given; and the abstract mentions searches of health technology assessment websites that the Methods do not describe.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Search methods; Methods › Search methods for identification of studies; Appendices 1 to 4
reporting_issues.consequence: The 2009 search cannot be reproduced from the article.

reporting_issues.issue: Several included trials fall outside the stated population of people with alcohol dependence and withdrawal symptoms: Spies 2003 (DSM-IV alcohol abuse, dependence excluded), Saitz 1994 (abuse or dependence), and trials of insomnia, anxiety or mood after detoxification (Ansoms 1991, Kolin 1981, McLendon 1980, Mielke 1976, Overall 1973). Table 5 and the list of benzodiazepines also include 'Abecamil' (Anton 1997); if this is abecarnil, it is a beta-carboline rather than a benzodiazepine (editors' note from general pharmacology, to be checked against the trial).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Types of participants; Characteristics of included studies; Results › Included studies, Table 5
reporting_issues.consequence: Some pooled estimates mix acute withdrawal with post-withdrawal symptom treatment; claims about acute withdrawal should note the trials that contribute.

reporting_issues.issue: Subgroup construction and labels: Additional table 2 lists paraldehyde and pentobarbital as Kaim 1972's anticonvulsant comparators, but Analysis 2.1.2 (seizures against anticonvulsants) enters only the paraldehyde arm (1 of 55), while Analysis 2.1.1 uses all 142 comparator patients; Additional table 2 also lists promazine, a phenothiazine antipsychotic, among Golbert 1967's anticonvulsant comparators; and the forest plots label Kramp's trial 'Kramp 1976' where the text, tables and reference list give 1978.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML (Additional table 2; Analyses 2.1 and 2.2, forest-plot images; Characteristics of included studies)
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor: the anticonvulsant subgroup for seizures leaves out one barbiturate arm, and the classification of comparators cannot be taken from the additional tables alone; the pooled comparisons against all other drugs are unaffected.

verification.source_read: PMC full text PMC12414628 (Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2010, issue 3, CD005063, DOI 10.1002/14651858.CD005063.pub3, the assigned DOI; the page notes it is an update of the 2005 version): all sections, both summary-of-findings tables, the comparison Tables 1 to 6, the Data and analyses tables, the characteristics of included, excluded and awaiting studies, Appendices 1 to 5, contributions of authors, sources of support and declarations of interest read as text. The 55 figures are images: the forest plots for Analyses 1.1, 1.2, 1.3, 2.1, 2.2, 2.3, 2.5, 2.6, 2.11, 2.12, 2.13, 4.1, 5.2, 5.3, 5.4 and 5.5 (566 pixels wide) were viewed enlarged on screen and their counts checked against the printed totals; the flow chart, risk-of-bias graph and summary and the other forest plots were not read. The included trials were not read. The PMC record links no correction, erratum or later version.

disagreements.first_pass: Per-trial counts were read from the Analysis 1.1 image (566 pixels wide, enlarged on screen) and add up to the printed totals. No single trial was significant on its own (Kaim 1969, RR 0.14, 0.02 to 1.09). The image labels the largest trial 'Kaim 1972', but its group sizes are those of Kaim 1969. In Sellers 1983 everyone with past withdrawal seizures also received phenytoin.
disagreements.reviewer: Claim writer's report (AI reader 173), checks: the two withdrawal reviews disagree on one trial, Naranjo 1983 (0 of 21 against 1 of 20 in Amato et al.; 0 of 15 against 2 of 15 in Mayo-Smith).
disagreements.resolution: Both counts confirmed by the second readers (AI reader 193 on the Mayo-Smith render; AI reader 200 on the Cochrane forest plot) and present in the claim anchors. Recorded on both cards as a discrepancy between the sources.

disagreements.first_pass: The review never states whether the CIWA-Ar and HARS values it pooled are scores at the time point or changes from baseline. The forest plots label a negative difference as favouring the comparator (other drugs, clonidine, symptom-triggered schedules), and the text reads them the same way; that is correct only if the values are reductions from baseline. In Analysis 5.4 the values for Spies 2003 (19.8 and 18.8) are of the size of reductions from an entry score above 20, while those for Daeppen 2002 in the same analysis (2.8 and 3.9) could be either.
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 200, corrected: 'never states' is too strong; the Results paragraph on fixed against symptom-triggered schedules labels the 48-hour CIWA-Ar result a change from baseline, and the Discussion speaks of change from baseline for HARS; better that the review never says so for the pooled analyses and its few statements do not fit all printed values. Substance confirmed (19.8/18.8 and 2.8/3.9).
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after finding both passages in the saved full text (Results › Effects of interventions, fixed versus symptom-triggered paragraph; Discussion › Summary of main results). Issue rewritten; consequence kept.

disagreements.first_pass: PMC HTML, Methods › Measures of treatment effect;
disagreements.resolution: Location of the Results passage added.

disagreements.first_pass: no EconLIT strategy is given; the EMBASE strategy's combination lines refer to line numbers that do not match its list; and the abstract
disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 200, corrected: the EMBASE combination lines do match; PMC renders Appendix 3 as a list numbered 1 to 23, and lines 4, 7, 21, 22 and 23 point to the right lines. Drop that part.
disagreements.resolution: Accepted after counting the lines of Appendix 3 in the saved full text: line 4 = 1 or 2 or 3, line 7 = 5 or 6, line 21 = 8/20 OR, line 22 = 4 and 7 and 21, line 23 = limit 22. The EMBASE clause removed; the rest of the issue confirmed.

disagreements.reviewer: AI reader 200, missed: Kaim 1972's pentobarbital arm is missing from Analysis 2.1.2; promazine listed among Golbert 1967's anticonvulsant comparators; 'Kramp 1976' label.
disagreements.resolution: Checked Additional table 2 in the saved full text (Kaim 1972: paraldehyde, pentobarbital; Golbert 1967: promazine, paraldehyde with chloral hydrate) and the second reader's saved Analysis 2.1 image (Kaim 1972: 2/142 in 2.1.1, 1/55 in 2.1.2; label 'Kramp 1976'). Added as one reporting issue. Which Golbert arm enters Analysis 2.2.2 could not be identified on the low-resolution image and is not stated.
